title: People Are Ghosting Long-Term Partners. Some Don’t Regret It
gist: A culture piece on ghosting spreading from casual dating-app encounters into long-term, multiyear relationships, citing survey data that 84% of millennials/Gen Z have been ghosted and that Gen Z is far more likely to sever contact with family or loved ones outright, alongside a new 'chief breakup officer' service and academic research on ghosting's psychological toll.

themes.theme: Ghosting is expanding from dating apps into long-term relationships

insights.claim: According to a Thriving Center of Psychology survey cited in the article, 84 percent of millennials and Gen Z say they've been ghosted at the end of a relationship, though ghosting has traditionally been far less typical for multiyear relationships than for early-stage dating.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Quantifies how normalized ghosting has become among younger cohorts even as the piece documents its spread into longer-term, previously more accountable relationship contexts.
insights.locator: According to a Thriving Center of Psychology survey

insights.claim: Vogue UK reported in late June on the trend of 'the disappearing boyfriend,' documenting women grappling with a partner's sudden, unexplained disappearance, often occurring even when the relationship seemed to be going well.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Indicates ghosting of established, seemingly-stable long-term partners is being recognized as a distinct, newly named cultural phenomenon by mainstream media beyond WIRED's own reporting.
insights.locator: In late June, Vogue UK shed light on the trend

insights.claim: Dating.com has begun offering a paid 'chief breakup officer' service, charging $3,000 a month for someone to end other people's relationships on their behalf.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: A concrete, monetized product response to relationship-avoidance culture — a small but telling commercial signal of how far outsourcing emotional labor around breakups has gone.
insights.locator: Dating.com recently announced that it was hiring a chief breakup officer

insights.claim: A Talker Research survey found that Gen Z are more likely than older generations to sever contact entirely with a family member or loved one without explanation — 60 percent compared to older generations — extending the ghosting pattern beyond romantic relationships.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Suggests ghosting is not confined to romantic dynamics but reflects a broader generational shift in Gen Z's approach to ending relationships of all kinds without closure.
insights.locator: A recent survey by analytics firm Talker Research

themes.theme: Psychological framing and social media aestheticization

insights.claim: Arizona State University communication professor Liesel Sharabi says Gen Z has grown up with dating apps and social media, making ghosting feel like a normal part of the dating experience even though it is hurtful, and argues digital communication has made ghosting 'easier and potentially more socially acceptable' at the cost of losing the humanity and decency people would want shown to them.
insights.speaker: Liesel Sharabi (via Jason Parham)
insights.so_what: Frames ghosting as a structural byproduct of app-mediated relationship formation among a generation that never knew dating without digital mediation — relevant context for platforms and products serving Gen Z relationship dynamics.
insights.quote: We risk losing the humanity and decency we would want someone to show us when ending a relationship.
insights.locator: Sharabi adds that digital communication has made ghosting

insights.claim: Los Angeles therapist Becca Hansel frames ghosting from an attachment-theory perspective as a 'nervous system strategy' used by people with avoidant or disorganized attachment patterns, for whom emotional closeness or conflict can feel threatening or overwhelming, though she notes it can also be a legitimate way to exit an unsafe or abusive situation without needing to justify the decision.
insights.speaker: Becca Hansel (via Jason Parham)
insights.so_what: Offers a clinical framework distinguishing ghosting-as-avoidance-pathology from ghosting-as-safety-strategy, useful for understanding the behavior isn't monolithic in cause or moral weight.
insights.quote: If someone doesn't feel emotionally or physically safe, I don't think they owe the other person an explanation.
insights.locator: In some cases, ghosting is a means of escaping

insights.claim: TikTok trends have aestheticized ghosting and estrangement, with young people posting videos feigning total detachment about ex-partners, and some extending the trend to ghosting friends, parents, or their 'entire bloodline' as a form of boundary-setting content.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Illustrates how social platforms are turning a socially costly interpersonal behavior into shareable, performative content, potentially reinforcing and normalizing it further among younger users.
insights.locator: They often aestheticize estrangement by turning heartbreak

insights.claim: A 2025 study published in Computers in Human Behavior found that ghosting has significant cognitive consequences for both the ghoster and the person ghosted, with the ambiguity and uncertainty of ghosting creating more persistent adverse psychological effects than straightforward rejection.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Provides an academic evidentiary basis that ghosting is measurably worse for long-term psychological wellbeing than direct rejection, countering the perception that ghosting is a 'painless' exit strategy — including for the person who initiates it.
insights.locator: According to a 2025 study published in Computers in Human Behavior
